judgments.title: LEE BEE EIM v SREEHAARAN A/L RAVINDRAN & ors
judgments.catchwords: 1 . This is one of two appeals arising from a road traffic accident. At the Sessions Court, the First Plaintiff, Sreehaaran a/l Ravindran, was riding a motorcycle with the Second Plaintiff, Durshini a/p Saravanan, as his pillion passenger. The Defendant, Lee Bee Eim, was driving a motorcar. 2. Following a full trial, the learned Sessions Court Judge, by her decision dated 12 June 2025, apportioned liability for the accident equally between the First Plaintiff and the Defendant, at 50% each. The learned Judge further found the Defendant 100% liable in respect of the Second Plaintiffs claim and dismissed the Defendant's counterclaim against the First Plaintiff, with costs. 3. Dissatisfied with different aspects of that decision, both sides appealed to this Court. In Civil Appeal No. PA-12B-20-06/2025 ("Appeal No. 20"), the First Plaintiff challenges the apportionment of liability at 50:50. In Civil Appeal No. PA-12B21-06/2025 ("Appeal No. 21"), the Defendant challenges the finding that she was 100% liable for the Second Plaintiffs claim and the dismissal of her counterclaim against the First Plaintiff. 4. As both appeals arise from the same accident and the same decision of the Sessions Court, they were heard together. 5. This judgment relates to Appeal No. 21 and the parties are referred to as they were in the Sessions Court.

judgments.title: Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Berhad v Ang Eng Hooi & ors
judgments.catchwords: (1) in a unilateral and written undertaking given by one party, X (X’s Unilateral Undertaking), to another party (Y) with regard to a debt settlement agreement between Y and Z (Settlement Agreement) - (a) is X’s Unilateral Undertaking valid or void? In this regard, whether the Contracts Act 1950 (CA) applies to X’s Unilateral Undertaking. If the CA applies to X’s Unilateral Undertaking, was there “consideration” for X’s Unilateral Undertaking as understood in s 2(d) CA?; and (b) if X’s Unilateral Undertaking was valid - (i) whether ss 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act 1950 (EA) bar the admissibility of extrinsic evidence to contradict, vary, add to or subtract from the contents of X’s Unilateral Undertaking; and (ii) how should the court construe and enforce the contents of X’s Unilateral Undertaking?; and (2) upon a court’s removal of a private caveat over a piece of land, whether the registered proprietor of the land (Land Owner) can claim compensation from the caveator under s 329(1) of the National Land Code (NLC) for - (a) all legal fees incurred by the Land Owner to apply to court for the removal of the private caveat; (b) the higher interest rate imposed by a lender on the Land Owner allegedly due to the entry of the private caveat; (c) the higher construction cost incurred by the Land Owner with regard to the Land Owner’s construction of a building on the land, purportedly as a result of the entry of the private caveat; and (d) loss of potential business suffered by the Land Owner allegedly due to the entry of the private caveat.

judgments.title: HILLMANLEO SDN.BHD v A.RAHIS SDN.BHD & ors
judgments.catchwords: 1. This is the Plaintiffs application in Enclosure 5 for an injunction directing the 2nd Defendant to pay directly to the Plaintiff, into the client account of the Plaintiffs solicitors, the sum of RM939,690.21. The application arises in the context of the Plaintiffs substantive claim against the Defendants in this action. 2. In essence, the Plaintiffs case is that it carried out works for the benefit of the 2nd Defendant at the behest of the 1st Defendant. The 1st Defendant is the main contractor for the relevant project. The Plaintiff contends that monies payable by the 2nd Defendant to the 1st Defendant include monies attributable to the work carried out by the Plaintiff and that those monies ought therefore to be channeled directly to the Plaintiff rather than paid to the 1 Defendant. 3. The Plaintiff characterizes the application as one concerning the manner of payment rather than the determination of its substantive entitlement. Its concern is that the 1st Defendant may receive monies from the 2nd Defendant without thereafter forwarding to the Plaintiff the amount attributable to the work it claims to have carried out. 4. The 1st Defendant opposes the application. Its fundamental position is that the Plaintiffs entitlement to RM939,690.21 is itself disputed and has not been adjudicated upon. The 1st Defendant further relies upon its pleaded case that the Plaintiff had agreed to accept RM333, 146.95 as full and final settlement of its claims relating to the works and expenses up to 19 December 2025. 5. The 2nd Defendant also opposes the application. Its position is that the contractual arrangements are between the 1st and 2nd Defendants and that it has no contractual obligation to pay the Plaintiff directly. It disputes the Plaintiffs asserted entitlement to payment from it.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya v SYAFWANA TRADING & ors
judgments.catchwords: Criminal Law—Money laundering—Forfeiture of property—Application under s 56(1) read with ss 58 and 61(2) of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 where no criminal charge or prosecution instituted under s 4(1)—Whether civil proceeding in rem directed at legal character of property—Applicable standard of proof—Whether civil standard on a balance of probabilities applies throughout to every element including predicate offence of cheating under s 420 of the Penal Code—Whether Public Prosecutor's statutory satisfaction under s 56(1) properly formed where Notice of Motion filed after all supporting affidavits affirmed and evaluated cumulatively—Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001, ss 4(1), 56(1), 56(4), 58, 61(2), 70—Penal Code, s 420 Criminal Law—Money laundering—Forfeiture of property—Commingling and instrumentality—Whether the entire credit balance of an officially dormant partnership bank account is forfeitable under ss 56(1)(d) and 56(2)(a)(iv) where tainted online scam proceeds are commingled with unexplained high-velocity Cash Deposit Machine deposits and repeated mule-account transfers—Variance in sums across three-layer banking trail and same-day statement sequence—Whether forensic ringgit-for-ringgit tracing required—Distinction between active commercial trading accounts and dormant front accounts repurposed wholesale as laundering conduits—Whether court empowered to order private restitution to scam victim or whether third-party claims governed by Gazette notice procedure under s 61(2)—Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001, ss 56(1)(d), 56(2)(a)(iv), 61(2) Criminal Law—Money laundering—Bona fide purchaser for valuable consideration without notice — Defence under s 56(2)(b) read with ss 61(3) and 61(4)—Whether five statutory limbs under s 61(4) are cumulative and conjunctive—Registered partners surrendering unfettered control of dormant partnership account to operational manager without inquiry into massive unexplained inflows—Whether wilful blindness defeats good faith—Whether sham invoices can retrospectively purify property tainted upon receipt—Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001, ss 56(2)(b), 61(3), 61(4) Evidence—Admissibility and weight—Statutory statements—Statements recorded from mule-account holder under s 32(2) of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001—Whether admissible as substantive evidence under s 40 notwithstanding absence of cross-examination—Assessment of probative value where statement against penal and legal interest corroborated by bank's prior Suspicious Transaction Report restriction and objective documentary record—Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001, ss 32(2), 40 Evidence—Burden of proof—Documentary evidence—Shifting of evidential burden under s 106 of the Evidence Act 1950 once illicit inflows into dormant entity established—Failure of respondents to produce accounting ledgers, tax filings, or supplier records to explain remaining balance—Whether expert forensic document examiner required to reject commercial invoices suffering patent internal absurdities on their face—Evidence Act 1950, ss 3, 106 Evidence—Affidavit—Admissibility, severability, and hearsay—Affidavits resisting forfeiture affirmed by non-partner operational manager of conventional partnership—Distinction between operational factual witness with direct personal knowledge under s 60 of the Evidence Act 1950 and third-party proprietary claimant under s 61 of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing, and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001—Absence of written Power of Attorney and use of corporate title—Whether objectio

judgments.title: SABITHA BAGAM BINTI KAPAL MARICAN v MAHADI BIN BADRUL ZAMAN & ors
judgments.catchwords: Contract - Financial financing agreement - Qard Hassan - Hibah - Fixed contractual return - Whether agreement constituted moneylending - Whether agreement Shariah-compliant - Whether fixed hibah amounted to interest and riba - Moneylenders Act 1951, ss 2, 5, 10O(a), 17A - Contracts Act 1950, ss 24, 66. Moneylending - Unlicensed moneylender - Presumption of moneylending business - RM1 million advanced for one year with fixed return of RM280,000 - Hibah payable in fixed instalments - Whether transaction a loan at interest notwithstanding Islamic nomenclature - Whether agreement void and unenforceable. Islamic law - Qard Hassan - Hibah - Requirement that hibah be voluntary and unconditional - Fixed and guaranteed hibah stipulated in agreement - Whether arrangement contrary to Shariah principles - Whether contractual hibah constituted riba al-nasi'ah. Illegality - Void contract - Admissions and estoppel - Acknowledgment of indebtedness by defendant's solicitors - Whether admissions precluded defence of illegality - Whether estoppel can validate unlawful agreement - Public policy. Restitution - Unjust enrichment - Void agreement - Recovery of principal sum notwithstanding illegality - Applicability of s 66 Contracts Act 1950 - Distinction between void profit element and recoverable capital - Whether lender entitled to restitution of monies advanced. Evidence - Burden of proof - Alleged third-party project - Absence of documentary evidence tracing funds - Whether defence established that funds were expended on project - Adverse inference. Practice and procedure - Quantification of restitution - Whether hibah already received to be deducted from principal sum recoverable - Net restitution - Double recovery.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.catchwords: Civil procedure — Bifurcated trial — Separate liability and quantum stages — Oral decision on liability — Subsequent alteration of liability findings during quantum proceedings — Functus officio — Whether judge became functus officio upon delivery of oral decision or upon perfection and sealing of final order — Correction of judicial error — Natural justice — Procedural fairness — Prejudice arising from alteration of liability findings — Assessment of damages — Substantive propriety of alteration — Appellate intervention — Consequential orders — Jurisdiction and power of High Court.

YA Dato' Che Mohd Ruzima Bin Ghazali

judgments.title: ROSLI A/L JENDUT & ors v AGROBEST (M) SDN. BHD & ors
judgments.catchwords: Notice of Appeal filed by defendants against the whole of the High Court’s decision eventhough the dismissal of the plaintiffs’ claim for special and exemplary damages were in defendants favour — whether plaintiffs ought to have filed a Notice of Appeal if they had wanted to appeal against the dismissal of their claim for special and exemplary damages —-Rules 5,8, 1A, 102, 103, 104, 105 Rules of Court of Appeal 1994 (RCA 1994), s 69(5) Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (CJA) —Proof of the Indigenous People of their connection to the deceased persons’ tombstones and grave sites — use of oral tradition and narratives under s 32(1)(d) and (e) Evidence Act 1950 (EA) — locus of the plaintiffs to sue for trespass for the demolition and desecration of their ancestors’ tombstones and grave sites —- nature of customary title — whether it has been extinguished before the alienation and issuance of land titles to private corporations —- effect of a 4(2)(a) National Land Code (NLC) on the law for the time being in force on customary tenure — whether Article 5(1) on right to life covers the protection of the indigenous peoples’ burial sites, custom and tradition —United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and its use in interpreting Constitutional Rights.
coram: YA Dato' Nordin Bin Hassan
YA Dato' Seri Vazeer Alam bin Mydin Meera
YA Dato' Lee Swee Seng

parties.label: PLAINTIF
names: FIRST WORLD HOTELS & RESORTS SDN. BHD.

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: LAU YEE SUM (BERAMAL DI BAWAH NAMA DAN GAYA PERUNDING JUTERA)
LEE YONG CHIEW (BERAMAL DI BAWAH NAMA DAN GAYA YC LEE ARCHITECT)
ZAHIRUDDIN BIN ZAINAL ( BERAMAL DI BAWAH NAMA DAN GAYA ZAHIRUDDIN TOWN PLANNING SERVICES)

judgments.catchwords: Tort — quia timet action by neighbouring landowners to restrain a proposed highland mixed development — claims in breach of statutory duty, private nuisance, trespass and negligence — safety and stability of shared Class III and Class IV slopes — whether excavation, piling and slope-cutting at the toe of the slopes threatened loss of natural lateral and vertical support to adjoining land, occupied hotel complex and access road — expert evidence, court-appointed expert, weight and independence of party experts — planning law — whether a valid and subsisting planning permission and development order existed under Part IV of the Town and Country Planning Act 1976 — lapse of planning permission under s 24 for failure to commence development in the specified manner within twelve months — whether demolition, site clearance, notices or subdivision constituted lawful commencement — earthworks and building plan approvals under the Street, Drainage and Building Act 1974 and the Uniform Building (Pahang) By-Laws 1996 — contravention of the Guidelines on Development Planning in Hills and Highlands and the National Physical Plan — Special Management Area exemption — private road — possession, control and regulation of access — natural right of support under s 44(1)(b) of the National Land Code — collateral challenge and second actor principle — remedies — declarations, prohibitory and mandatory injunctions, restoration of the toe of the slopes, general damages — aggravated and exemplary damages refused — counterclaim for losses, delay, idleness and reputational harm dismissed — costs on a party and party basis.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Hajah Aliza binti Sulaiman
